title: MCP server
snippet:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI tools connect to external platforms. The Plain MCP server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` lets tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor work with your support data directly. You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user. No API keys needed.

### ChatGPT
In ChatGPT, add the official Plain plugin:
1. Open the [Plain plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6aec88addd3c8191bc0daa4b3fff3a4c) and add it
2. Sign in with your Plain account and choose your workspace
3. In a chat, type **@** and pick **Plain**
### Cursor
You can add the Plain MCP to Cursor via your Cursor config at `~/.cursor/mcp.json`
```
{
"mcpServers": {
"plain": {
"type": "remote",
"url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"
}
}
}
```
Go to **Cursor Settings** → **Tools & MCP** and click **Connect** next to Plain to authenticate.
### Claude.ai
1. Go to “Customize” → “Connectors”
2. Click the ➕ icon, then choose “Add custom connector”
3. Add a custom connector named “Plain” with the Remote MCP server URL `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`
4. Click the “Connect” button next to the newly created Plain connector to authenticate.

### Claude Code
Adding the Plain MCP to claude-code can be done via the `mcp-remote` helper package which involves adding the following to your `~/.claude.json` configuration.
```
"mcpServers": {
"plain": {
"command": "npx",
"args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"],
"enabled": true
}
}
```
Unfortunately Claude Code does not support refreshing OAuth tokens yet. A workaround until that is implemented is to use the `mcp-remote` npm package. Next time you start Claude Code, it will launch a browser window asking you to authenticate with your Plain account and select the workspace you’d like to connect. Run the `/mcp` command and select the `plain` MCP to see more details.
### **FX**
[**fx**](https://fx.sh/) is a terminal AI coding agent from Vercel Labs. Add the Plain MCP via the CLI:
```
fx mcp add --transport http plain https://mcp.plain.com/mcp
```
Or add it manually to `~/.fx/mcp.json`:
```
{
"mcp": {
"plain": {
"type": "http",
"url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp",
"enabled": true
}
}
}
```
fx will prompt you to complete the OAuth flow with your Plain account on the next session start.

Plain MCP uses OAuth to allow your MCP server connection to share the same context as your normal web app user. No additional managing of permissions required. T

title: Set up Plain for a person
snippet:
You are an agent setting up Plain, a customer support platform, for the person you’re working with. You do the setup through Plain’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`, which signs in as that person with OAuth. Don’t ask the person for an API key: the MCP server needs none, and an API key belongs to a machine user, not to them. Follow the steps in order. Steps 1 to 4 only read. In step 5, nothing in the workspace changes until the person agrees to it. When the person has to choose, such as which labels to create or which Slack channels to connect, use your host’s question tool if it has one, such as `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code. Otherwise ask in chat. When you’ve handed the person something to do, such as signing up or approving Slack, and they say they’re done, check it with a tool if you can, then move straight on to the next step.

1. Check for an existing connection
If Plain tools are already loaded in your session, call `getMyWorkspace`. When it returns a workspace, tell the person its name and ID and ask whether it’s the workspace they want to set up. A connection is bound to one workspace, so it might be the wrong one. If it is the right one, go to step 4. If no Plain tools are loaded, ask whether the person already has a Plain workspace. If they do, or they gave you a workspace ID (it starts with `w_`), go to step 3 and check after connecting that `getMyWorkspace` returns that workspace. Otherwise, or if `getMyWorkspace` fails with `No workspace ID provided`, start at step 2.
##
​
2. Have the person sign up and create a workspace
The person signs up themselves. You can’t create an account or a workspace for them. Send them this link and wait for them to say they’re done:
```
https://app.plain.com/get-started
```
Tell them to:
1. Sign up with Google or their work email
2. Name their workspace when Plain asks
3. Come back to you once the workspace exists
Don’t connect the MCP server before the workspace exists. The connection gets bound to an account with no workspace, every tool fails with `No workspace ID provided`, and the person has to reconnect.
##
​
3. Connect the Plain MCP server
Add the server for the host you’re running in. Every host opens a browser window for the person to sign in to Plain and pick the workspace. The person must finish that sign-in themselves.
###

title: Plain's MCP Server: Connect Any AI Tool to Your Support Data
snippet:
Plain now has an MCP server. If you use Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or any other AI tool that supports the MCP standard, it can talk directly to your Plain workspace. Your threads, your customers, your help center, all accessible from the AI tools you already have open.
Here's the same scenario with Plain's MCP server connected:
You open Claude, type "What's going on with this customer?", and it pulls their recent threads, looks up their profile, checks the tenant's other threads, finds the relevant help center article, and drafts a response with the right details. One prompt instead of ten minutes of digging.

With Plain's MCP server connected, your AI tools can do the same things you do in Plain's UI, on your behalf. We built 30 tools across five areas:
1. **Threads.** Fetch, search, reply, assign, snooze, change priority, add labels, mark done, create internal notes. The daily workflow stuff that eats your time when you're doing it manually across dozens of threads.
2. **Customers.** Look up profiles, search by name or email, pull a customer's full thread history.
3. **Tenants.** Search and manage company-level data. Spot patterns across all of a company's threads. Useful when you're trying to figure out whether an issue is a one-off or part of something bigger.
4. **Help center.** Browse articles, find stale content, create or update articles directly. You can flag articles that haven't been updated in 90 days and draft new ones from recurring questions.
5. **Workspace.** Access your user profile, workspace settings, and available labels.
## BYOA and MCP: two sides of the same idea
Last month we launched Bring Your Own Agent: [connect any AI agent](https://www.plain.com/blog/connect-any-ai-agent-to-plain) to Plain's infrastructure. This month, MCP.
**BYOA is about what happens inside Plain.** Your AI agent triages threads, replies to customers, manages queues. It works autonomously within your support workflow.
**MCP is about what happens outside Plain.** The AI tools your team already uses (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) can now reach into Plain alongside your other work tools. Support data lives in the same conversation as your code, your bugs, and your team chat.
## Where the real value shows up
Plain on its own gets you thread lookups and customer context. Add GitHub, Linear, Slack, and other platforms through MCP and the AI can trace a customer issue from ticket to pull request to deploy to team channel without you opening any of them.

title: MCP for Customer Support: Platforms and Permissions (2026)
snippet:
MCP for customer support means your support platform runs an MCP server, so the AI client your team already uses (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) can read customer context and act on threads through one standard interface, without an integration layer you build and maintain.

Plain is the agentic infrastructure for customer work, a B2B customer support and help desk platform, and its MCP server signs each person in with their own Plain account over OAuth, so a connection carries that person's permissions and no one else's. As of November 2026, [Plain's MCP server](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/mcp-server) has **400+ tools**.
## What is MCP for customer support?
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems. A platform runs an MCP server that describes its tools: a name, a description and an input schema for each. An AI client connects, authenticates and calls those tools when a request needs them, so nobody has to write code against the platform's API first.

|---|---|---|---|
| Plain MCP server | OAuth only, each person once per client | The signed-in person's Plain role; replies and actions appear under that user | [Plain help article](https://help.plain.com/article/does-the-plain-mcp-server-support-api-key-authentication-h7d83qtfdzxo4h49x4oyklwx) |

Plain's [MCP server docs](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/mcp-server) say the server "has the same permissions as your user," and that replies to threads "will appear as though they come from your user." The help article adds the part buyers ask about most:
- **An admin's connection is the admin's alone.** Each person who uses the server completes the OAuth flow once in their own client. There is no shared credential that lets several people connect, so an admin connecting Claude doesn't hand admin access to anyone else.
- **Any role can connect, including Viewer.** Viewer seats are unlimited on every Plain plan, so an engineer or account manager can pull support context into their own AI client without a paid seat, and their connection carries a Viewer's permissions.
- **Every action is attributed.** Replies and actions appear under the user who made them, as they do in the app, which ties MCP activity to a real person for audit and attribution.

title: plainframework.com/docs/plain-mcp/plain/mcp/README.md
snippet:
# plain.mcp
**Expose your Plain app to AI clients as an MCP server over HTTP.**

An MCP server is a subclass of [`MCPView`](https://plainframework.com/docs/plain-mcp/plain/mcp/views.py?llm#MCPView) that declares a list of `MCPTool` subclasses. `MCPView` is a Plain View — you mount it directly in your URLs.
```python
# app/mcp.py (auto-discovered on startup)
from plain.auth.views import AuthView
from plain.mcp import MCPTool, MCPView
class Greet(MCPTool):
"""Say hello to someone."""
def __init__(self, name: str):
self.name = name
def run(self) -> str:
return f"Hello, {self.name}!"
class AppMCP(MCPView, AuthView):
name = "myapp"
login_required = True
tools = [Greet]
```
Mount it:
```python
# app/urls.py
from app.mcp import AppMCP
from plain.urls import Router, path
class AppRouter(Router):
namespace = ""
urls = (path("mcp/", AppMCP, name="mcp"),)
```
AI clients connect to `https://yourapp.com/mcp` using the [Streamable HTTP transport](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports#streamable-http).
`name` is required. `version` defaults to `settings.VERSION` (from your `pyproject.toml`). Auth and authorization are covered below.
## Requests and results
MCP `2026-07-28` is **stateless** — no handshake, no sessions, no server-to-client stream. Every POST carries one self-describing JSON-RPC request, so the client restates who it is on each call, in `params._meta`:
| `params._meta` key                           | Required | Value                           |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------- |
| `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`    | yes      | `"2026-07-28"`                  |
| `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` | yes      | object                          |
| `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`         | no       | `{"name": ..., "version": ...}` |

MCP clients handle all of this — you only assemble it by hand when poking at your own server:
```bash
curl -X POST https://myapp.com/mcp \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \
-H 'Mcp-Method: tools/list' \
-d '{
"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list",
"params": {"_meta": {
"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
}}
}'
```

```python
from plain.mcp import MCPTool, MCPView, OAuthResourceServer, TokenInfo
class AppTool(MCPTool):
mcp: AppMCP  # forward ref — typed access to AppMCP's user, scopes, etc

title: Plain's MCP
snippet:
**Update, November 2026:** Plain’s MCP server now has 400+ tools. See the [MCP server docs](https://www.plain.com/docs/integrations/mcp-server) for the current list.
You can now connect AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor directly to your Plain workspace using the Plain MCP server. Once connected, your AI assistant can read threads, look up customers, check tenant details, and browse your help center. It can also take actions: reply to threads, assign them, change priority, add labels, create notes, and mark threads as done.
At launch, the server included 30 tools across threads, customers, tenants, help center articles, and workspace data. You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user.
To get started, check out the [setup guide](https://plain.support.site/article/mcp-server).
